extracted.intended_audience: media researchers, communication scholars, and students/journalists interested in news selection and foreign news structure
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical and empirical criteria for what makes events in foreign affairs become news: a set of factors (12 in the study), hypotheses about how they combine (additivity, complementarity, exclusion), and operational coding dimensions used in content analysis of foreign-news cuttings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworthiness is additive across factors: events score along multiple factors and total score determines admission as news (the additivity hypothesis focuses on type 1 — prominent news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An event does not have to score maximum on any single factor; high values on several factors add up to produce prominence. Example: a high Fi and a high Fj together create prominent news; low on both excludes news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementarity hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event is low on one factor it must be high on some other factor to become news (applies to type 2 — ordinary news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With many possible factor combinations (66 pairwise hypotheses for 12 factors), a low score on Fi increases the probability that some Fj is high; complementarity explains how different factors can compensate for each other to achieve newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Events low on relevant factors are excluded from news (focuses on type 3 — events not news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exclusion hypothesis complements additivity and complementarity by characterizing the conditions under which events fail to reach the newsworthiness threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trichotomy of events (Type 1/2/3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of events into three kinds according to two factors Fi and Fj: Type 1 Prominent news (both high), Type 2 Ordinary (one high, one low), Type 3 Events not news (both low).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a simple illustrative model: with two factors one can see how combinations map to prominence; generalizes to many factors in empirical testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial threshold / scoring model
rubrics_metrics.description: News acceptance is determined by whether an event's total score across factors exceeds a floor level (example: floor at score 6 yields many combinatorial ways to pass).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why many different factor combinations can produce news and why operating factors may not be obvious to the public (large number of combinations such as (162)=924 ways to reach threshold).

rubrics_metrics.name: H1: Cultural distance → elite-focused reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The more distant the nation (culturally), the higher the tendency to report elite action (i.e., report top leaders/elite rather than rank-and-file people).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized and tested by counting rank of people reported and quoted; expectation: distance reduces identification with rank-and-file and increases elite concentration in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: H2: Rank of person → negativity (negativism by rank)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower the rank of the person, the more negative the event (common people are more often presented in negative contexts than elites or top leaders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized by coding mode of event as -1 (negative) or +1 (positive) and averaging by rank levels (top leader, elite, common people); tested across countries and crises — found strong confirmation in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: H3: Distance → negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: The more distant the nation, the more negative the event (distant nations/events are more likely presented negatively).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tested using causal-agent coding and mode; evidence in this study is mixed/inconclusive — not strongly confirmed nor disconfirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: H4: Cultural distance → required relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: The more culturally distant the theater, the more relevant the event must appear to be (distant events must be 'made relevant' to be reported).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevance is often achieved by linking the distant event to familiar perspectives (e.g., motherland-colony, East-West) so the story fits the readers' frames and news criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency condition for distant nations (pair 1,4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more distant a nation is, the more will an event have to satisfy the frequency criterion (i.e., be abrupt/attention-capturing) to be recorded as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: distant-nation coverage privileges sudden, dramatic events (natural disasters, accidents, changes of government) and underreports slow-build quantitative developments; leads to image of these countries as abrupt/dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity/clarity requirement for distant events (pair 4,3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more distant an event, the less ambiguous it will have to be (it must be simple) to make news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remote/strange events are presented in 'ideal types' or simplified terms; complexity tolerated within one's own culture but not at a distance; fosters stereotyped, homogenous images of distant nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance/expectation requirement for distant nations (pair 4,5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more distant the nation, the more consonant the news must be (it must fit patterns of expectation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that match stereotypes (e.g., coups in Latin America) pass filters more easily, while stories that contradict expectations are less likely to be reported (may be seen as fake or atypical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity effect lowers threshold (pair 7,2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher the continuity effect, the lower the threshold for follow-up news about the same topic (once a channel is open, subsequent items enter more readily).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates 'news strings' and artificial continuities because the channel remains open for related follow-ups even at lower criterion values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition effect lowers threshold (pair 8,2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher the composition effect (under-representation of categories), the lower the threshold can be to include items so as to represent those categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In lulls of foreign news, the newsworthiness limit may drop to include low-scoring items to fill representational gaps, producing images of discontinuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency importance for positive events (pair 1,12)
rubrics_metrics.description: The less negative the news (i.e., more positive), the more important the frequency condition: positive events must be especially brief/ceremonial to appear as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive developments are often telescoped into events (ceremonies) and augmented by elite presence and PR; this underreports gradual positive work by non-elite actors and biases perception of how change occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of reporting (negativity/positivity/neutral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding dimension: whether a cutting reports something 'negative' (destroyed/disrupted) or 'positive' (built/constructed) or neutral; mode correlates with rank and other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compute indices ranging from -1 to +1; neutral/both/neither items often omitted from some analyses. Negative contexts are more frequent for lower ranks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank of people reported (personalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding dimension: top leader, elite, common people (also categories: no people, underdog/topdog); degree to which news concentrates on elites versus rank-and-file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by presence and frequency of quotes and mentions; elite and top leaders are quoted far more often; common people are rarely quoted (e.g., 2 of 612 Cyprus cuttings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal-agent attribution and mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Who is presented as the causal agent of events and whether they are shown causing negative or positive events — lower-rank agents are less likely to be shown causing positive events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top leader and elite often pooled in analysis; results showed consistent pattern that lower rank correlates with being attributed negative causal agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective/framing (e.g., motherland-colony, East-West, UN-colony, intra-colony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding dimension: the perspective or frame used in presenting the story (linking theater to broader political frames increases relevance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most frequent perspective in crises studied was 'motherland-colony'; framing choices determine how distant events are made relevant to readers and influence perceived importance and focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus of story (economic/political/social/cultural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding dimension describing the principal focus of the news story: economic, political, social or cultural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the sample, focus varied from economic (Cuba) to political (Congo, Cyprus), aligning with real developments; focus interacts with perspective and other factors in news selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source dependency / press-agency dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Criterion that news content and images depend heavily on dominant news agencies (AP, UPI, Reuters, AFP); 'own correspondent' is often insignificant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Norwegian sample, four foreign agencies accounted for ~87% of items; agency presence biases which angles and frames are available to local papers and thus shapes selection and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit-of-analysis operational variables (contextual vs. proper variables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological rubric: code contextual variables referring to the newspaper (name, party color, date) and proper variables referring to the cutting itself (presentation, length, type, source, person quoted, items present/absent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishing these variable types allows testing hypotheses across newspapers (replication) and across cuttings (content features); sample design selected four papers to provide dispersion for replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication-by-newspaper design
rubrics_metrics.description: Design principle: select newspapers across axes (morning/afternoon, radical/conservative) to provide dispersion so findings that hold across all four receive stronger confirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not a content criterion per se but an evaluative design standard used to assess robustness of observed patterns across differing editorial contexts.
